title: R.E.P.O. items and tools explained
description: A practical item index grouped by what each tool changes during a run.
lead: Read the item pool by job: damage, control, movement, carry protection, healing, and information. The right tool is the one that fixes the current route, not the one with the highest community tier.
steps: Start with the item category: weapon, throwable, drone, staff, healing, or information.
Compare what the item changes for the crew: damage, time, distance, weight, durability, or recovery.
Separate permanent upgrades from run-only tools, and check the current item description after a patch.
Pair each tool with a situation: fragile heavy loot, blocked doorway, enemy control, revive, or low-health return.
Before relying on an exact price or duration, confirm it in the current shop or item description.
mistakes: Copying a price from an old guide, treating a mod entry as vanilla behavior, and describing an item without saying when to use it.
versionNote: Community item databases are useful for vocabulary and structure, but prices, pools, ammo, and effects need current-client checks.

title: When to save or spend in R.E.P.O.
description: A simple budget rule for upgrades, tools, and risky extra loot.
lead: Spend when the purchase removes the reason you failed. Save only when the shop roll does not solve the next risk or when buying would leave the team without a basic recovery option.
steps: Name the next run’s biggest bottleneck before opening the shop.
Buy a survival or carrying upgrade when it directly increases the chance of meeting quota.
Keep enough budget for a tool that changes a known enemy or extraction problem.
Do not hoard through several shops if the same weakness keeps ending runs.
Record the purchase, the run result, and whether the change paid for itself in safer value.
mistakes: Saving by default, buying every visible item, and comparing prices without comparing the time or risk the item removes.
versionNote: Prices and shop pools vary by level and version. Community discussions are evidence for questions, not universal rules.

title: Apex Predator (Duck): create space before you counter
description: The Duck dossier: recognize the threat, protect the carrier, and avoid a bad chase.
lead: Treat the Apex Predator as a route problem first. Call its location, move the valuable out of its line, and only use a dedicated counter when the team has a clear exit.
steps: Call “Duck” with the room and direction as soon as the team recognizes it.
Stop carrying through the threat area and put the valuable somewhere recoverable.
Split the team: one player watches the route while the carrier rotates toward the cart or extraction.
Use the item or environment counter only after the escape route is clear.
Treat exact triggers, chase behavior, and player-count interactions as version-sensitive unless you can confirm them in your current build.
mistakes: Chasing it with the valuable still in hand, stacking the team in one doorway, and assuming a single counter works in every map.
versionNote: Monster behavior and counter reliability are version-sensitive. Use this as conservative route advice rather than an exact timing reference.

title: Trudge: route around the pull
description: Keep large valuables and the return path out of the danger zone.
lead: Trudge turns a narrow route into a physics problem. Give the carrier an alternate line, stop feeding heavy items into the pull, and use control only when it creates a real window.
steps: Call Trudge and identify the open side of the room or hallway.
Drop or park the valuable before the pull can move it into a wall or pit.
Move the scout first and make a visible return route for the carrier.
Use a control tool or a strong counter only when the team can finish the carry during its duration.
Test heavy-object behavior separately from player behavior; the patch changed how Trudge handles larger valuables.
mistakes: Trying to out-pull it while holding a fragile item, fighting in a doorway, and forgetting the cart is part of the escape route.
versionNote: Official v0.4.4 notes changed Trudge’s suck behavior, so older footage is useful for ideas but not for exact timing.

title: Tick: do not carry blindly
description: A small threat becomes dangerous when the carrier loses control of the item.
lead: Ticks punish the player who keeps holding loot without checking the threat. Put the object down, create space, and make the next action deliberate.
steps: Call the Tick and stop moving the valuable while the team identifies who is being pressured.
Put the item down in a safe position instead of trying to sprint-carry through contact.
Use a wall, cart, or open room to separate the carrier from the threat.
Resume the carry only after the team has a clear route and the item is stable.
If Tick behaves differently while holding, dropping, or countering, prioritize the current game behavior over older guide claims.
mistakes: Running while holding the item, turning into a wall, and assuming a small enemy can be ignored because it is not a boss.
versionNote: Community guides disagree on some attack conditions and damage details. Use the conservative handling rule here and treat exact triggers as version-sensitive.

title: Duo strategy: split focus, not the run
description: A two-player plan for scouting, hauling, callouts, and extraction.
lead: In a duo, one player should not be both blind scout and carrier. Give each person a job, use short callouts, and retreat before one mistake becomes a lost run.
steps: Before leaving the truck, choose a carrier and a scout; swap only at a safe handoff point.
Use the scout to clear the next room and call the return route, not to wander out of voice range.
Keep the cart near the current work area so the carrier is not making empty trips.
At an enemy alert, the scout calls the route while the carrier drops the item and follows.
For extraction, the carrier finishes the point while the scout watches the return and truck.
mistakes: Both players carrying at once, losing proximity voice, and waiting until quota is barely met to plan the return.
versionNote: Role recommendations are strategy guidance, not game rules; map layout, monster density, and player skill change the best split.

title: Team roles for 3–6 players
description: Assign scout, hauler, distractor, extractor, and recovery jobs before danger appears.
lead: More players only help when the team has distinct jobs. Keep the carrier protected, keep one person responsible for the return path, and avoid six people making the same call.
steps: For three players, use one scout, one hauler, and one flexible support who can carry or watch the rear.
For four players, add a dedicated extractor or distractor so the carrier can stay focused.
For five or six players, keep two carriers but preserve one scout and one recovery/defense role.
Use a fixed callout format: room, item or enemy, action.
Before activating extraction, name who stays on the route and who returns to the truck.
mistakes: Everyone looting, nobody owning the return route, and letting proximity voice break the team into isolated pairs.
versionNote: The role matrix comes from community strategy guides and should be adjusted for the current map, player skill, and patch.

title: Common beginner mistakes in R.E.P.O.
description: Twelve repeatable failure patterns and the correction for each.
lead: Most early wipes are not caused by a missing secret. They come from rushing fragile items, fighting every monster, skipping the shop, and losing the return plan.
steps: Walk by default while carrying; sprint only for a clear escape.
Use the cart early and keep fragile items out of repeated hand-to-wall collisions.
Do not fight every monster. Hide, route around, or wait when the threat has no clean counter.
Buy the upgrade or tool that fixes the last failure instead of saving by habit.
End each run from a safe truck or shop state and record the one mistake to remove next time.
mistakes: Rushing fragile items, using movement upgrades without a landing plan, ignoring the radar/map, and treating every room as loot that must be taken.
versionNote: Some advice in community beginner lists reflects current snapshots; keep hard numbers and save behavior version-tagged.

title: Levels and objectives: what changes between runs
description: Plan around map identity, quota pressure, and the next difficulty spike.
lead: Do not memorize one route and call it a plan. Track the map’s structural character, the extraction layout, the valuables you can safely move, and the point where monster pressure changes.
steps: Identify the map and its stable shape: tight vertical rooms, open sightlines, holes, or long returns.
Mark extraction points and the safe staging area before spending time on low-value rooms.
Use the first rooms to learn the current run’s loot density and threat pressure.
Treat later levels as an efficiency check: fewer empty trips, safer carry paths, and clearer roles.
Keep the objective, route, and failure point in mind so the team can adjust on the next level.
mistakes: Assuming procedural layouts are fully memorized, judging a map only by loot value, and entering a difficulty spike with the same team plan.
versionNote: Map layouts vary, while each map’s broad structure is more stable. Use route principles rather than relying on fixed coordinates from another run.

title: Headman Manor: route, risks, and extraction plan
description: A focused map guide for a vertical, cluttered, high-collision layout.
lead: Headman Manor rewards a cautious staging plan. Clear a route through the vertical rooms, use the cart to protect fragile value, and leave noisy or awkward valuables until the return path is known.
steps: Find the main stair and the safest cart staging point before chasing high-value rooms.
Clear doorways and corners for large objects before attempting a heavy carry.
Treat noisy valuables as an alert decision: call the room, prepare the retreat, then pick up.
Use vertical shortcuts only when the landing and recovery route are visible.
Finish the safest extraction points first and reserve the return route for the crew, not extra loot.
mistakes: Trying to move a piano or clock through a blind corner, carrying without a cart staging point, and assuming a high room is worth the fall risk.
versionNote: Map-specific routes need current screenshots or footage. This page uses community map descriptions and is a route framework, not a fixed seed.

title: Valuable routes and safe carry plans
description: Plan the trip around staging, handoffs, and return safety instead of item value alone.
lead: A valuable route is a sequence of safe handoffs: room to cart, cart to extraction, extraction to truck. The best item is the one the crew can deliver without turning the return into a second mission.
steps: Choose a staging point near the current rooms and outside the most likely enemy route.
Prioritize valuables by value, fragility, distance, and the number of hands needed.
Move fragile items one at a time and use a callout before every doorway or corner.
Keep the return route clear; never stack the cart where it blocks the only escape.
Once quota is met, stop adding route length and convert the safe staging area into a return plan.
mistakes: Ranking loot only by price, carrying several fragile items at once, and leaving the cart behind while the team explores deeper.
versionNote: Exact route maps require a seed, screenshot, or current-client recording. The article publishes the route method and marks map-specific claims for verification.

title: Carrying and physics tips
description: The small movement choices that preserve item value and team time.
lead: R.E.P.O. turns carrying into a route mechanic. Hold the item close, rotate before tight turns, walk through fragile sections, and use a cart or tool when the object is larger than the hallway.
steps: Practice grab, rotate, pull, and gentle drop on a low-value object before handling expensive loot.
Keep heavy or fragile items close to the body and slow down before a doorway or corner.
Use the mouse wheel or equivalent rotation control to set the object flat before placing it.
Load fragile items into the cart early and use a second player for heavy or awkward objects.
Use a low-value object to check collision, damage, and vehicle interactions before risking expensive loot.
mistakes: Running while carrying, throwing fragile loot for speed, dropping on an edge, and assuming an item is safe because it is inside the cart but sticking out.
versionNote: Physics interactions are unusually version-sensitive; official patches have changed carts, vehicles, staffs, and item handling.

title: Health, Stamina, and Range: when each matters
description: Choose the stat that changes your route instead of buying a generic comfort pick.
lead: Health buys forgiveness, Stamina buys actions, and Range buys safer interaction distance. Compare the failure each stat removes against the cost and the role that receives it.
steps: Choose Health when one mistake or one hit repeatedly ends the run.
Choose Stamina when the carrier or scout loses time to repeated sprint, climb, or movement downtime.
Choose Range when reaching from a safer angle changes how you collect or control objects.
Give the stat to the role that uses it most: carrier, scout, or recovery player.
Run one comparable route after the purchase and record time, damage, and delivered value.
mistakes: Calling one stat universally best, comparing old prices, and buying Range without a route where distance actually matters.
versionNote: Effect summaries are stable strategy guidance; exact increments and price ranges must be retested on the current build.

title: R.E.P.O. v0.4.4 patch notes: what changed for players
description: The v0.4.4 update improves melee handling at higher Strength, adds one second of protection after revival, updates all staffs, and makes Trudge more disruptive around large valuables.
lead: The biggest v0.4.4 changes affect recovery and object control. Revived players get a brief safety window, melee weapons respond more firmly at higher Strength, all staffs use six battery pips, and Trudge now pulls large valuables with Void Staff-style suction.
steps: Melee weapons now scale their handling correctly with Strength. Higher Strength should make them feel firmer, but it does not replace spacing or a safe attack angle.
A revived player receives one second of invincibility. Use that moment to move out of immediate danger; do not treat it as a long damage window.
All staffs now have six battery pips. Zero Gravity Staff is more controllable on non-enemy objects and can move the user when self-cast.
Roll Staff makes rolling objects target enemies, while self-use gives the player camera-steered rolling. Void Staff pulls heavy objects more strongly and creates outward surges near its center.
Trudge now uses Void Staff-style suction, pulling larger valuables more easily and creating more chaos near the center. Park important loot farther from its pull lane.
mistakes: Assuming the revive protection lasts long enough to stand still, leaving heavy valuables near Trudge, and using old staff battery or behavior advice after updating.
versionNote: Official v0.4.4 notes were published May 25, 2026. Check the version shown by the game before applying these changes to a later build.

title: R.E.P.O. v0.4.4 returning player checklist
description: Returning to R.E.P.O. after v0.4.0? Relearn melee handling, revive timing, staff batteries and object control, vehicle buttons, and Trudge suction.
lead: If your habits were built around v0.4.0, the v0.4.4 changes most likely to surprise you involve Strength-based melee handling, the one-second post-revive safety window, six-pip staffs, improved staff control, and Trudge pulling larger valuables.
steps: Try one melee weapon at your current Strength before committing to a close-range fight; handling now becomes firmer as Strength increases.
After a revive, use the one-second invincibility window to escape the danger area and regroup rather than starting a long attack.
Recheck staff charges before a mission. All staffs now use six battery pips, and their object-control behavior changed across the v0.4.x updates.
Use extra care when grabbing a vehicle near its button: the interaction area was reduced to limit accidental activation.
Give Trudge a wider safety radius around valuable objects. Its Void Staff-style suction can catch larger loot and behaves more chaotically near the center.
mistakes: Relying on muscle memory from v0.4.0, expecting old staff behavior, or parking the cart and large valuables inside Trudge’s pull lane.
versionNote: This checklist reflects the official v0.4.4 announcement dated May 25, 2026. Later versions should take priority if your main menu shows a newer build.

title: R.E.P.O. upgrade planner
description: Choose a crew role and the problem that ended your last run to get one upgrade priority, a fallback, and a practical check for the next attempt.
lead: Use the interactive planner below. It gives decision support rather than a fixed tier list, and it never assumes a shop item is available.
steps: Select the crew size, the role receiving the purchase, and the failure that ended the run.
Read the primary priority and compare it with the upgrades or tools actually available at the Service Station.
Use the fallback when the first category is unavailable or the role does not need it.
Follow the next-run check to see whether the purchase solved the named problem.
Change one variable at a time; choose a different failure only when the previous bottleneck is no longer ending runs.
mistakes: Choosing a universal tier-list favorite instead of the current bottleneck, buying a team tool without assigning a user, and changing several unrelated variables at once.
versionNote: The planner avoids fixed prices, caps, and guaranteed shop availability because those details can change by version and run.

title: R.E.P.O. monster counter cheat sheet
description: A fast first-response checklist for sight, sound, proximity, grab, and object-control threats.
lead: Identify the trigger before choosing a counter. Put the valuable down without blocking the retreat lane, call the threat, then use cover, distance, silence, or a prepared control tool.
steps: For a sight or gaze threat, break line of sight behind solid cover and avoid staring to confirm it.
For a sound-sensitive threat, stop sprinting, jumping, hard drops, and noisy item handling until the team has a route.
For a proximity or charge threat, create open space and sidestep only after its approach or wind-up is clear.
For a grab or pull threat, call the victim’s direction and keep teammates and valuables out of the same danger lane.
For an object-control threat such as Rugrat or Trudge, secure the valuables first. Fight only if the enemy blocks the route and the crew has a tested counter.
mistakes: Calling only the enemy name without its direction, fighting while carrying fragile loot, and stacking the team in one doorway.
versionNote: Use the visual enemy index for individual dossiers. Exact damage, timing, spawn tier, and item interactions remain version-sensitive.

title: R.E.P.O. FAQ: quota, extraction, upgrades, monsters, and co-op
description: Direct answers to common early-run questions, with links to the full guides for each system.
lead: Quota tells you how much value the current objective needs; extraction and leaving are separate steps. Buy around the failure ending your runs, and treat monsters as route problems before treating them as fights.
steps: Do I need to clear the whole map? No. Satisfy the displayed objective and leave when the extra loot is not worth the route risk.
Why can’t we leave after reaching quota? Confirm every required extraction point has resolved, then regroup at the truck and follow the current departure prompt.
What should I buy first? Choose the upgrade or tool that addresses the repeated failure: carrying, stamina, damage, reach, control, or fragile value.
Should we fight every monster? No. Identify its trigger, protect the loot lane, and fight only when it blocks the route and the crew has a safe setup.
How should co-op roles work? Assign navigation, carrying, and lookout duties, but let players switch when the room or current load changes.
mistakes: Treating quota as a full-clear order, assuming one purchase order fits every crew, and chasing a monster after the route is already safe.
versionNote: Prompts, shops, enemy behavior, and multiplayer interactions can change. The linked focused guides carry the version-specific caveats.

title: What is R.E.P.O.? Story, setting, and confirmed details
description: R.E.P.O. is an online co-op horror game where physics-based valuables must be retrieved and extracted while monsters threaten the crew and its cargo.
lead: The game casts players as Semibots sent to retrieve valuable objects from abandoned environments. The immediate story is communicated through the Taxman, objectives, locations, and environmental details; explanations beyond what the game or developer confirms should be treated as interpretation.
steps: The official premise is retrieval: locate valuable, fully physics-based objects and extract enough value to satisfy your creator.
The Semibots work as a crew, with the gameplay supporting up to six online players.
The Taxman frames quota and progression, but the game leaves much of the wider world and the fate of its human spaces implicit.
Rooms, props, valuables, shop interactions, and enemy designs provide environmental clues without establishing every fan theory as canon.
When a theory explains the creator, locations, or monsters, separate what appears on screen from what the community infers.
mistakes: Presenting a fan theory as confirmed lore, treating a joke or item description as a complete timeline, and confusing gameplay terminology with an official story explanation.
versionNote: This page stays with the official premise and visible environmental storytelling. Future developer statements or major updates may add confirmed context.
